newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Prosecutor seeks leniency for Srebrenica killer.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutor seeks leniency for Srebrenica killer.

text.p: A U.N. war crimes prosecutor recommended on Wednesday that the punishment meted out to a Bosnian soldier who took part in a massacre of Moslems from Srebrenica in 1995 should be limited to a jail term of 10 years.

Prosecutor Mark Harmon of the U.S. urged the U.N. war crimes tribunal to show leniency to Drazen Erdemovic, because he had turned himself over to the tribunal, confessed, shown remorse and provided valuable information about war crimes.

"The prosecutor recommends leniency in the case of Mr Erdemovic. If it is the decision of this honourable court to impose a term of imprisonment, we would respectfully recommend that it not exceed 10 years," Harmon said.
Defence lawyer Jovan Babic said his client had been forced to take part in the summary execution against his will and should therefore face a jail term of no more than one year.
Erdemovic, 24, will be the first person sentenced by the Hague-based tribunal and the first sentenced by an international war crimes tribunal of any sort for almost half a century.
Presiding judge Claude Jorda of France said the tribunal would hand down its verdict in two weeks' time.
Created by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, the Hague tribunal may pass a maximum sentence of life imprisonment but may not impose the death penalty.
Harmon said Erdemovic, who is a Bosnian Croat but served in the Bosnian Serb army, had been the first insider from the Bosnian Serb military to testify in public about Srebrenica.
"His testimony exposed the lies of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders that the killings of civilians from Srebrenica was nothing but Moslem propaganda," he said.
Erdemovic pleaded guilty in May to taking part in the slaughter of 1,200 unarmed Moslem men after the "safe haven" of Srebrenica fell to the Bosnian Serbs in July 1995.
He said the victims were taken in buses to Branjevo farm at Pilica, near Zvornik, where they were shot in groups of 10 by his unit of the Bosnian Serb Army.
But he insisted that he had no choice but to take part in the five-hour killing spree as the officer in charge had threatened to kill him if he did not carry out the order.
"The massacre at Branjevo farm was amongst the largest crimes committed during the tragic conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina," Harmon said.
Erdemovic, by his own admission, had played a significant role in that crime, he added.
But Erdemovic had also shown courage, he said, by testifying at public hearings in July against deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former military chief General Ratko Mladic.
Both men have been charged with genocide for the killings after the fall of Srebrenica but both remain free.
Harmon said Erdemovic would have remained a "faceless, nameless executioner" and the tribunal would never have heard of the Pilica massacre if Erdemovic himself had not spoken out.
Information he provided had led to the discovery of 140-160 bodies at a mass grave near the farm, despite subsequent attempts by the Bosnian Serbs to remove the evidence, he said.
Erdemovic was given the last word on Wednesday and spoke of his regret at the deaths on all sides of the war in Bosnia.
"I have lost many good friends of many nationalities...They were not in favour of war...they simply had no other choice. This war came and there was no way out and the same happened to me," he said.
